:::{#thm-descent-direction}
#### A short enough step downhill decreases the function

Let $f : \reals^p \to \reals$ have first partial derivatives
that are continuous on $\reals^p$ ([continuity](vector-calculus.qmd#def-continuous-several)),
and let $\vx \in \reals^p$ be a point with $\vecf{g} \eqdef \deriv{\vx} f(\vx) \ne \vzero_{p \times 1}$.
Then there is an $\bar{s} > 0$ with $f(\vx - s \vecf{g}) < f(\vx)$ for every $s \in (0, \bar{s})$:
a short enough step in the descent direction $-\vecf{g}$ (@def-descent-direction) decreases $f$.

:::

::: proof

Let $h(s) \eqdef f(\vx - s \vecf{g})$.
The inner function $s \mapsto \vx - s \vecf{g}$ has derivative $-\tp{\vecf{g}}$ ([vector-valued derivative](vector-calculus.qmd#def-vector-valued-derivative)),
so by the vector chain rule ([vector chain rule](vector-calculus.qmd#thm-chain-vec))

$$
\ba
h'(s)
&= -\tp{\vecf{g}}\,\deriv{\vx} f(\vx - s \vecf{g}),
&& \text{(chain rule)}
\\
h'(0)
&= -\tp{\vecf{g}}\,\deriv{\vx} f(\vx)
&& \text{(set } s = 0 \text{)}
\\
&= -\dprod{\vecf{g}}{\vecf{g}}
&& \text{(definition of } \vecf{g} \text{)}
\\
&= -\norm{\vecf{g}}^2
&& \text{(squared length)}
\\
&< 0.
&& \text{(} \vecf{g} \ne \vzero_{p \times 1} \text{)}
\ea
$$

Since $h'(0) = \lim_{s \to 0} (h(s) - h(0)) / s$ is negative,
taking $\tolout = \abs{h'(0)}$ in the definition of the limit gives an $\bar{s} > 0$
such that $(h(s) - h(0)) / s < h'(0) + \abs{h'(0)} = 0$ for $0 < s < \bar{s}$.
Multiplying by $s > 0$, $h(s) < h(0)$, that is, $f(\vx - s \vecf{g}) < f(\vx)$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-descent-direction}
#### How short is short enough

In @exm-gradient-descent, $f(x) = x^2$ at $x \ne 0$ has $g = 2x$, and
$f(x - 2 s x) = (1 - 2s)^2 x^2 < x^2$ exactly when $\abs{1 - 2s} < 1$, that is, when $0 < s < 1$.
So @thm-descent-direction holds with $\bar{s} = 1$,
and the step $s = 1.5$ of that example was too long.

:::
